### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **UNEP — United Nations Environment Programme** on 2024-02-14, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

Used Heavy- Duty Vehicles and the Environment: A Global Overview of Used Heavy-Duty Vehicles: Flow, Scale and Regulation This Used Heavy- Duty Vehicles and the Environment: A Global Overview of Used Heavy-Duty Vehicles: Flow, Scale and Regulation report analyses the flow and scale of used heavy-duty vehicles (HDVs) from three major used HDVs exporters – Japan, the European Union (EU) and Republic of Korea (ROK). It also reviews the regulatory environment for used HDVs import in 146 countries, 122 of which are low- and middle- income countries (LMICs). The major exporters of HDVs (used & new) are the EU, Japan, Republic of Korea (ROK), Mexico, the US, and China. However, while China manufactures 67% of global HDVs, its share of used HDV exports was only 8% in 2020. This is changing rapidly as the policy to expand used vehicles exports is being implemented and from 2022 more than 30 cities in China have been approved to export used vehicles globally. The EU on the other hand exported about 46% of used HDVs (2020) while contributing to about 6% of global HDVs manufacturing. Thus, while the worldwide HDV manufacturing market shifted from Western Europe and North America to emerging economies in the last two decades, used HDVs exporters are primarily high-income economies. george.maina@un.org Wed, 02/14/2024 - 16:07

title: Mustang to pilot clean heating solutions as Nepal tackles black carbon emissions
summary: Kathmandu, 10 August 2026 – Across Nepal’s high mountain regions, many families still rely on firewood and other biomass fuels to keep warm during long and harsh winters. While this remains one of the few affordable options for many households, it...
body:
### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **ICIMOD — International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development** on 2026-08-10, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

Kathmandu, 10 August 2026 – Across Nepal’s high mountain regions, many families still rely on firewood and other biomass fuels to keep warm during long and harsh winters. While this remains one of the few affordable options for many households, it also exposes families to indoor air pollution and contributes to black carbon emissions that accelerate the melting of snow and ice in the Hindu Kush Himalaya. To address this challenge, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), in partnership with the Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC) and Practical Action Nepal, has launched the Harnessing Renewable Energy for Clean Heating in the Himalaya (HEARTH) project, with support from the Clean Air Fund. The project will work with communities in Mustang to identify, test and promote clean heating technologies that can provide reliable warmth without relying on traditional biomass fuels. It aims to generate practical evidence on what works in the high-altitude environments and support efforts to make the clean heating more accessible and affordable for mountain households and institutions. For families living in Nepal’s mountains, cleaner heating could mean warmer homes with less smoke, improved indoor air quality, reduced dependence on firewood, and lower pressure on local forests. The project will also contribute to efforts to reduce black carbon emissions, a major short-lived climate pollutant that affects air quality and contributes to glacier and snow melt across the region. “People living in the mountains face some of the harshest winters in Nepal, yet many households still rely on firewood to keep warm,” said Pema Gyamtsho, Director General at ICIMOD. “This affects both their health and the fragile mountain environment. By working with communities to identify cleaner heating options, we hope to demonstrate that staying warm, protecting health, and reducing climate-warming emissions can go hand in hand.” “AEPC considers the HEARTH Project a strategic opportunity to generate evidence that will inform future policies, financing mechanisms, and market development for clean, non-biomass heating solutions in Nepal’s high-altitude regions,” said Nawaraj Dhakal, Executive Director of AEPC. “The experiences and lessons from the Mustang pilot will provide valuable insights into identifying heating technologies that are technically feasible, economically viable, and socially acceptable. These findings will support Nepal’s energy transition by promoting climate resilience, strengthening energy security, reducing dependence on traditional biomass, and improving the quality of life of mountain communities.” Mr. Dhakal also emphasized the need for the HEARTH Project to incorporate a comprehensive sustainability and post-project support strategy. Despite significant progress in expanding access to electricity across Nepal, clean heating remains a major gap in the energy transition of mountain regions. High upfront and operational costs, limited availability of suitable technologies and after sales service and challenging climatic conditions continue to constrain adoption. Through HEARTH, partners will assess heating needs in home and public institutions, demonstrate suitable technologies, monitor impacts on indoor air quality and black carbon emissions, strengthen local technical capacity, and engage suppliers, financial institutions, and policymakers to support longer-term uptake. There is no just transition without mountain clean heating. Nepal has achieved 99% electricity access, yet 80% of rural households still rely on traditional biomass for cooking and heating, leaving the intense, cold-weather heating demands of high-altitude mountain regions dangerously neglected. ICIMOD is closing this critical gap by supporting scaling of market-ready, non-biomass space heating across Nepal’s high-altitude areas. By replacing traditional fuels with clean electric and thermal heating, this project aims to boosts use of local renewable energy, reduce black carbon emissions and indoor air pollution for the mountain communities. For media inquiries, please contact: Neraz Tuladhar (Raz), Media Officer Email: media@icimod.org The post Mustang to pilot clean heating solutions as Nepal tackles black carbon emissions appeared first on ICIMOD .

title: Local governments back long-term support for climate adaptation in Roshi and Dhankuta
summary: Kathmandu, 12 August 2026 – Two municipalities in Nepal have committed to integrating locally led climate adaptation solutions into their plans, programmes, and budgets, a move aimed at strengthening long-term support for vulnerable communities fa...
body:
### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **ICIMOD — International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development** on 2026-08-12, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

Kathmandu, 12 August 2026 – Two municipalities in Nepal have committed to integrating locally led climate adaptation solutions into their plans, programmes, and budgets, a move aimed at strengthening long-term support for vulnerable communities facing growing climate risks. Roshi Rural Municipality in Kavrepalanchok and Dhankuta Municipality have signed Letter of Intent with the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and its implementing partner, the Centre for Environmental and Agricultural Policy Research, Extension and Development (CEAPRED), to align the Integrated Climate Adaption Solutions for the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HI-CAS) project activities with municipal priorities and development plans. The commitment is expected to strengthen local ownership of adaption efforts and create pathways for sustainability through municipal programmes and investments. Launched in March 2026, the HI-CAS project is being implemented in Ward 1 and 2 of Roshi Rural Municipality and Ward 8 of Dhankuta Municipality. The project's Integrated Adaptation Solution Packages (IASP) combines springshed management, renewable energy to improve irrigation access, and agrobiodiversity conservation to address climate risks identified by local communities. The project integrates feminist and intersectional approaches to empower women, Indigenous Peoples, and marginalised communities in climate adaptation and resilience building efforts. “We all know that the impacts of a changing climate are often felt by women and Indigenous People, said Pema Gyamtsho, Director General of ICIMOD. “I am delighted to see the municipalities of Roshi and Dhankuta proactively participating in a project that seeks to strengthen the resilience of vulnerable communities, particularly women, girls, Indigenous Peoples and marginalised groups in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region.” Jessica Fullwood Thomas, Senior Project Coordinator of HI-CAS, said the municipalities’ commitment reflects the importance of locally led adaption. “This step recognises that adaptation solutions work best when they are rooted in the lived realities of the people and places, they are designed to serve and when local governments play a leading role,” she said. “We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the municipalities and CEAPRED and the municipalities to ensure that adaptation efforts respond to local needs, align with local priorities, and continue beyond the project lifetime of a single project.” Local leaders said the letters of intent reflect their commitment to supporting adaption efforts in their communities. “Roshi Rural Municipality is committed to providing the support needed for the implementation of HI-CAS, which is highly relevant in the current context,” said Dinesh Lama, Chairperson of Roshi Rural Municipality. Mayor Chintan Tamang of Dhankuta Municipality said the municipality is already promoting GESI -responsive springshed management and sees opportunities to expand their approach. "Dhankuta Municipality is eager to adopt these climate adaptation solutions and hopes to scale them up in the future.” Jaya Mukunda Khanal, Executive Director of CEAPRED welcomed the municipalities’ continued engagement. “We are very grateful to both local governments for their commitment and enthusiasm since the beginning of the project,” he said. “We hope to continue working together to strengthen these efforts.” The letters of intent also clarify roles and responsibilities among partners while strengthening coordination and alignment between the project and municipal development priorities. They reinforce commitments to GESI, springshed management, renewable energy, and agrobiodiversity conservation. The HI-CAS project is funded by the Government of Canada through Global Affairs Canada (GAC) and will run until the end of 2028. title: Local governments launch Nepal’s first-ever roadmap to revive and protect drying springs
summary: Kathmandu, 21 August 2026 – As global leaders gather in Stockholm, Sweden, for World Water Week 2026, nine local government leaders from three districts in Nepal, together with the Chair of the Municipal Association of Nepal, have endorsed and lau...
body:
### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **ICIMOD — International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development** on 2026-08-21, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

Kathmandu, 21 August 2026 – As global leaders gather in Stockholm, Sweden, for World Water Week 2026, nine local government leaders from three districts in Nepal, together with the Chair of the Municipal Association of Nepal, have endorsed and launched the country’s first sub-national roadmap for springshed management and governance. The roadmap is a locally owned plan to revive and protect drying springs that millions of Nepalis rely on for drinking water, household use, livestock rearing, and irrigation. The initiative comes at a critical time. Springs across Nepal are under increasing pressure from climate and human-induced factors, including land use change, deforestation, population growth, forest fires, overgrazing, and extreme weather events. In Kavrepalanchok district alone, citizen-science based mapping of nearly 5,700 water sources across seven municipalities and rural municipalities found that 58% of active springs are showing declining flow, while more than one-quarter have already dried up. Nationwide, only 16% of Nepal’s population has access to safely managed drinking water services (UN, 2024). For millions of rural families, this means longer walks to fetch water, increased workloads for women and children, and reduced agricultural productivity. The drying of springs is also a growing concern in other Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) countries, including Bhutan, India and Pakistan. About the roadmap This roadmap was co-developed with four municipalities and two rural municipalities in Kavrepalanchok district, two municipalities in Dhankuta district, and one municipality in Khotang district. It aims to: Strengthen local government capacity for springshed management Integrate Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI)-responsive springshed management into local policies, annual plans, and budgets Provide a model than can be adapted and scaled across Nepal’s hill and mountain municipalities Developed through the experiences, challenges, priorities, suggestions and recommendations of participating Local governments, the roadmap reflects a collaborative approach to addressing local water insecurity. This work is supported by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and funded by the UK and Australian Governments. title: Rasuwa border flood underscores need for stronger regional cooperation on climate risks, HKH lawmakers say
summary: THIMPHU, Bhutan, Aug. 26, 2026 – As news emerged of the devastating flood in Nepal's Rasuwa district along the Nepal-China border, parliamentarians from across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region on Wednesday said the tragedy underscored the urge...
body:
### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **ICIMOD — International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development** on 2026-08-26, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

THIMPHU, Bhutan, Aug. 26, 2026 – As news emerged of the devastating flood in Nepal's Rasuwa district along the Nepal-China border, parliamentarians from across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region on Wednesday said the tragedy underscored the urgent need for stronger regional cooperation to address climate risks that transcend national boundaries. At the opening of the 2nd Hindu Kush Himalaya Parliamentarians' Meet in Thimphu, parliamentarians, representatives, and members of the organising and supporting teams observed a moment of silence for the victims and their families. Participants said the disaster highlighted the importance of collective action, stronger preparedness, and sustained regional cooperation to reduce climate-related risks and build resilience across the HKH region. The two-day meeting, taking place from 26 to 27 August, brings together legislators from across the region to exchange experiences, discuss emerging climate risks, and explore how policies, legislation, and public investments can better support adaptation and resilience. Opening the meeting, Honourable Deputy Speaker Sangay Khandu of the National Assembly of Bhutan stressed the role of parliamentarians in turning climate commitments into action. "Resilience cannot live in scientific reasoning anymore or in the speeches of ministers and government officials or members of parliament. It cannot live only in the commitments we make at the global stage," he said. "Resilience should be carefully woven into the fabric of our laws, our budgets, our institutions and our actions on the ground. It is parliamentarians who have the power to ensure it." Participants highlighted that climate risks are increasingly affecting communities across borders and require coordinated responses that go beyond national efforts. Building on the momentum of the first HKH Parliamentarians' Meet held in Kathmandu in 2025, the gathering aims to strengthen political commitment and deepen regional collaboration on climate action, resilience, and inclusive development. "Last year, in Kathmandu, the first Hindu Kush Himalaya Parliamentarians' Meet established an important platform for parliamentary dialogue across the region. We shared knowledge, discussed common challenges, and called for stronger regional cooperation," said Pema Gyamtsho, Director General of ICIMOD. "Let us not forget that the decisions we make, or do not make, today will affect generations in the future. We have an opportunity to make a difference for them. This is what we expect from our gathering: to provide hope for future generations and create a pathway for a shared, prosperous and peaceful future for the HKH." Representatives from across the region shared perspectives on the importance of integrating climate adaptation into national development priorities while strengthening regional cooperation. "Bangladesh's National Adaptation Plan provides a clear framework for building resilience, but its success also depends on regional cooperation that can help us share knowledge, strengthen implementation and address the climate risks that connect the Hindu Kush Himalaya with downstream countries," said Muhammad Nawshad Zamir, Honourable Member of Parliament of Bangladesh. "It is an absolute honour to represent Nepal in the opening session of the 2nd Hindu Kush Himalaya Parliamentarians' Meet 2026. As the lead organiser for the first Hindu Kush Himalaya Parliamentarians' Meet in Kathmandu, Nepal, I feel inspired and excited to see parliamentarians' continuous engagement through the second edition of this meet," said Honourable Ashok Kumar Chaudhary, Chair of the Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee, Federal Parliament of Nepal. "Pakistan's experience shows that climate adaptation must be embedded in development planning, supported by adequate investment and informed by the realities of vulnerable communities. We need to move beyond responding to climate disasters towards anticipating risks and building resilience before impacts occur," said Her Excellency Dr Shezra Mansab Ali Khan Kharal, State Minister of Pakistan. "Stronger regional cooperation across the Hindu Kush Himalaya can help countries share knowledge, strengthen preparedness and scale up solutions, while ensuring that adaptation reaches the communities that need it most." title: Major flash flood sweeps through Nepal’s Rasuwa district, raising fears of further downstream flooding
summary: A major flash flood struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district on Wednesday morning, sending a powerful surge of water, sediment and boulders through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, raising concerns over further potential downstream impacts. "We a...
body:
### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **ICIMOD — International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development** on 2026-08-26, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

A major flash flood struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district on Wednesday morning, sending a powerful surge of water, sediment and boulders through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, raising concerns over further potential downstream impacts. "We are deeply saddened by this tragic disaster, which struck so suddenly and unexpectedly," said Pema Gyamtsho, Director General of ICIMOD. "We stand in solidarity with the people and Government of Nepal during this difficult time. Our thoughts and prayers are with the victims, their families and all those affected, and we are committed to providing support wherever possible." According to local reports, water levels in the Bhote Koshi basin began rising rapidly around 9:00 AM local time on August 26. The flood breached riverbanks and travelled downstream through the Bhote Koshi River into the Trishuli River, with potential impacts extending into Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Scientists from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and partner institutions in Nepal and China are investigating whether the flood may have been triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude area. Preliminary assessment based on video footage and information from affected areas suggest that a large volume of ice and rock debris may have entered the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River. Researchers say the event could have generated a sudden surge that carried water, sediment and large boulders downstream. Rapid rise in Trisuli River water level at Malekhu. Source: DHM. Hydrological observations indicate the exceptional speed and magnitude of the flood wave. Water levels on the Trishuli River at Galchchi reportedly rose by as much as nine metres within 30 minutes, while levels at Malekhu increased by seven metres over a similar period. Several water monitoring stations along the Trishuli River were reportedly damaged or washed away during the event, although the Glachchi monitoring station remains operational. Updated on 27 August: USGS recorded a magnitude 5.2 earthquake in the flood-hit region around the time of the reported avalanche. Source: USGS Experts are also assessing whether debris temporarily blocked the river at a narrow section, forming a landslide dam. Such blockage can create secondary hazard if impounded water is suddenly released. Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockage. Preliminary analysis of seismic records has identified unusual signals recorded during the period of the disaster. Data from a seismometer in Jilong, approximately 12 kilometres from the affected area showed anomalous signals, while a second station in Zhangmu also recorded unusual activity. Scientists are examining whether these signals are connected to the suspected avalanche. At present, no causal link has been established between seismic activity and the flood. "The same site devastated by last year's Rasuwa flood is once again under threat," said Qianggong Zhang, Head of Climate and Environmental Risks at ICIMOD. "An ice avalanche in the Lhende Khola is the suspected trigger, but the cause remains unconfirmed. With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border, authorities warn a second flood is imminent and evacuation orders are now in place for Jilong port." The flood has reportedly caused significant damage to infrastructure in the affected areas, including hydrological monitoring stations. Several hydropower facilities are located along the Bhote Koshi River and connected river systems. "The increasing frequency of cryosphere hazards is becoming more visible than ever before. The pace of change is so rapid that current efforts are struggling to keep up," said Mohd. Farooq Azam, Senior Cryosphere Specialist at ICIMOD. "Today's disaster in the Lhende Khola underscores the need for stronger regional collaboration, with governments taking coordinated action to respond to cross-border hazards." Experts at ICIMOD are continuing to analyse hydrological, seismic, remote-sensing and field data to better understand what triggered the event and assess ongoing risks to downstream communities. ICIMOD remains in close communication with the Prime Minister’s Office in Nepal, scientific institutions and partners in China as assessments continue. Scientists cautioned that while climate change is altering glaciers, snow conditions, permafrost and mountain slopes across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, it is too early to determine what role climate change played in this specific event. Additional quotes: "The same site devastated by last year's Rasuwa flood is once again under threat. An ice avalanche in the Lhende Khola is the suspected trigger, but the cause remains unconfirmed. With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border, authorities warn a second flood is imminent—evacuation orders are now in place for Jilong port." – Qianggong Zhang, Head of Climate and Environmental Risks, ICIMOD, Nepal "What we saw in the Lhende Khola is truly a catastrophe. It reminds me of the community-based early warning systems ICIMOD has been implementing with partners across the HKH, where upstream communities pass on flood information to those downstream, giving them time to prepare and move to safety. In this case, a cross-border early warning system could be a strong example of cooperation between the two countries. Our experience shows that providing information alone is not enough. Communities also need to be aware about how to translate this information and prepare themselves to act on it without panicking. This event is a hard reminder that in areas where such disasters are more likely, communities need to stay alert and stay prepared for the unforeseen." – Neera Shrestha Pradhan, Water and DRR Lead “Multi-hazard risks are increasing in the Himalayas and the Lhende Khola case is one such example. The exposure and risk profile of downstream communities including Rasuwa and Betrawati is changing dramatically. With these communities at the forefront, real time risk information needs to reach local decision-makers and translate into life-saving decisions.” – Basanta Raj Adhikari, Director, Centre for Disaster Studies, Tribhuvan University, Nepal "The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in fourteen months, this time most probably triggered by an ice avalanche blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream. This still needs to be confirmed, as we receive further information. These are cascading hazards: a cryosphere event becomes a flood in a settlement within hours."– Saswata Sanyal, DRR Specialist, ICIMOD, Nepal “The increasing frequency of cryosphere hazards is now visible more than ever. The pace is so fast that our ongoing efforts are not able to cope with this rapid change. Today's disaster in the Lhende Khola is another cause for regional collaboration where governments should take some joint, consolidated steps to react to such cross-border hazards" – Mohd. Farooq Azam, Senior Cryosphere Specialist, ICIMOD, Nepal For media inquiries, please contact: ICIMOD (Kathmandu) Claire Warmenbol, Head of Communications Raz Tuladhar , Media Officer Anshu Pandey , Senior Media Associate Email: media@icimod.org The post Major flash flood sweeps through Nepal’s Rasuwa district, raising fears of further downstream flooding appeared first on ICIMOD .

### 2. Ecosystem & Regional Impact
Within the Hindu Kush Himalaya context, unmitigated climatic and hydrological variability creates compound vulnerabilities for community adaptation buffers, seasonal agriculture, and water storage security. Institutional monitoring underscores the urgency of empirical baseline validation over static historical averages.

### 3. Policy, Engineering & Practitioner Implications
- **Evidence Verification**: Telemetry and field methodologies must align with peer-reviewed assessment frameworks.
- **Intervention Protocol**: Regional practitioners are advised to incorporate dynamic risk profiles into infrastructure planning and community disaster mitigation.

title: Standing in solidarity with the tragic Kyirong-Rasuwa flash flood victims
summary: I am deeply saddened by the tragic loss of lives and devastation caused by the sudden flash flood in Rasuwa, Bagmati Province, Nepal, and Xizang (Tibet), China. My heart goes out to the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives an...
body:
### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **ICIMOD — International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development** on 2026-08-27, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

I am deeply saddened by the tragic loss of lives and devastation caused by the sudden flash flood in Rasuwa, Bagmati Province, Nepal, and Xizang (Tibet), China. My heart goes out to the families and loved ones of those who have lost their lives and to all those enduring the consequences of this tragedy. I also extend my deepest appreciation to all those working tirelessly on the ground in response and rescue efforts. On behalf of ICIMOD, I extend our solidarity to the people and the Governments of Nepal and China at this difficult time. We stand ready to support the ongoing response and recovery efforts, drawing on the knowledge, science, data, and expertise available to us. The speed and force of the flood, carrying large volumes of water, sediment, and boulders through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, are deeply concerning. The potential for impacts further downstream is a reminder of how quickly a hazard in the mountains can become a wider regional concern. It also reinforces the importance of timely information, early warnings, preparedness, and coordinated action. I am writing this message from Bhutan, where I am attending the Second HKH Parliamentarians’ Meet. Being here at this moment makes the importance of regional cooperation feel even more immediate and personal. The tragedy in Rasuwa (Nepal) and Kyirong (China) reminds us that the mountains we share, the rivers that connect us, and the communities that depend on them cannot be separated by national boundaries. Neither can the risks we face. What happens in one part of the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) can have consequences far beyond it. This is why we need stronger cooperation, not only in times of crisis, but before disasters strike. We must share knowledge and data, strengthen early-warning systems, improve preparedness, and ensure that information reaches communities in time to save lives. Our gathering in Bhutan is therefore not simply about dialogue. It is about turning our shared understanding into collective action. Regional cooperation must move from aspiration to sustained action, because the risks are growing faster than any one country can address alone. The decisions we make today will shape the safety and well-being of generations to come. The people of the HKH deserve nothing less than our collective commitment to building a safer, more resilient future. At ICIMOD, we remain committed to standing alongside the Governments of Nepal and China and working with all HKH countries to strengthen science, preparedness, resilience, and regional cooperation. In moments such as this, solidarity must be more than words. It must translate into action, cooperation, and support. title: Hindu Kush Himalaya countries address implementation gaps in their climate actions
summary: Kathmandu, Nepal – With the aim of strengthening climate action reporting, 40 representatives from Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) countries gather in the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) from 1 to 3 September 2026 for t...
body:
### 1. Empirical Findings & Field Observations
According to authoritative reporting released by **ICIMOD — International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development** on 2026-09-04, regional environmental assessments indicate substantial operational shifts across local and transboundary ecosystems. 

Kathmandu, Nepal – With the aim of strengthening climate action reporting, 40 representatives from Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) countries gather in the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) from 1 to 3 September 2026 for the first capacity-building activity under the Hindu Kush Himalaya Regional Climate Action Transparency Hub (HKH-RCATH). Drawing experiences and lessons from the first Biennial Transparency Report (BTR 1) preparation in 2025, the workshop aims to strengthen regional peer learning and facilitate preparation of national GHG inventories for BTR2, through exchange of experiences, challenges, and good practices It also contributed to building a regional pool of practitioners connected to HKH ETF Hub. The insights and output will directly inform the design of a future, regionally tailored course, ensuring targeted capacity-building aligned with identified needs. “This gathering is particularly timely in the wake of the devastating events that unfolded last week in China and Nepal – two of ICIMOD’s regional member countries. These events are yet another stark reminder of the urgency and scale of the climate crisis confronting the Hindu Kush Himalaya. Since its establishment in December 2025, the HKH. Transparency Hub has provided an important platform for our regional member countries to come together, discuss common challenges in meeting their commitments under the Paris Agreement, and, most importantly, identify concrete actions to address the gaps and navigate these challenges collectively. This gathering is a solid demonstration of regional collaboration and solidarity, a shared commitment by our countries to stand together for a region that is among the world’s most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.” Pema Gyamtsho, Director General, ICIMOD. The BTRs are submitted under the Enhanced Transparency Framework (ETF) established under Article 13 of the Paris Agreement. Through the BTRs, countries regularly report information on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and removals, progress in implementing and achieving their nationally determined contributions, climate change impacts and adaptation, and financial, technology and capacity-building support provided, needed and received, as applicable. The framework builds trust and helps the global community measure progress toward climate goals. “UNFCCC secretariat welcomes this first activity of the HKH transparency hub as an important step in strengthening transparency and climate action across this climate-vulnerable region. The recent tragic event reminds us, in a very tangible way, of the importance of our work on climate change. It also underscores why reliable climate information, data and transparency matter – not only for understanding what is happening, but also for strengthening preparedness, informing decisions and helping countries respond to a changing climate. This makes our discussions here in Kathmandu particularly timely and relevant.” Xuehong Wang, Director, Transparency, UNFCCC. Experiences shared during the Regional Stakeholder Consultation Workshop in Paro (December 2025) highlighted common challenges, including limited institutionalised technical capacity and fragmented data systems for the preparation of national GHG inventories. Banking on this initial consultation, this workshop has carved concrete next steps through a shared work programme for the three-year MOU between ICIMOD and UNFCCC focussed on the operationalisation of the HKH RCATH. The first year was set out for the transparency hub establishment conducted in 2025. Implementation and capacity enhancement will be the focus of 2026, starting with this activity, the hub will facilitate continued engagements through workshops and technical meetings, peer learning and regional exchanges, resource mobilisation and partnerships and institutional coordination mechanism established among the HKH countries. It is planned that the third year will focus on scaling up and sustainability of these activities. The HKH Regional Climate Action Transparency Hub, established under the UNFCCC-ICIMOD Memorandum of Understanding, serves as a regional platform for sustainable capacity-building, and peer to peer leaning, among other things, to improve reporting under the ETF of the Paris Agreement while enhancing climate action.
